node.title: The Incidental Pulmonary Nodule
node.goal: Measure an incidental nodule to the Fleischner convention, judge solid from subsolid, and give the follow-up the guidance recommends or say why it does not apply.

quiz.prompt: A 63-year-old with a 40 pack-year smoking history has a CT pulmonary angiogram for pleuritic pain, negative for embolus. It shows a single solid nodule in the right lower lobe with a mean diameter of 4 mm, smooth margins and no calcification. There is no known malignancy and no immunosuppression. What does the 2017 Fleischner guidance recommend?
choices: An optional single CT at 12 months
A CT at 6 months and at 18 months
A CT at 3 months, then PET-CT
Immediate biopsy of the nodule
quiz.answer: An optional single CT at 12 months
quiz.explain: For a single solid nodule under 6 mm, low-risk patients need no routine follow-up, and high-risk patients are offered an optional CT at 12 months. The word optional carries the argument: even in a heavy smoker a nodule this size has under about a one per cent chance of being a cancer, so the recommendation is a discussion rather than an instruction, and features such as an upper lobe location, spiculation, coexisting emphysema or fibrosis, or a family history legitimately tip an individual decision. The 6 to 12 month schedule with a second scan at 18 to 24 months belongs to the 6 to 8 mm band, and going straight to PET-CT or biopsy at 4 mm subjects the patient to tests that cannot answer the question at that size. Note also what the study is: an incidental finding on a scan done for something else, which is the only setting the guidance addresses.

quiz.prompt: A first CT in a 60-year-old shows a solitary part-solid nodule in the left upper lobe, 14 mm overall with a 4 mm solid component. There are no symptoms of infection and no prior imaging exists. What is the next step?
choices: Repeat thin-section CT at 3-6 months
PET-CT to assess the solid component
CT-guided biopsy of the solid part
Lobectomy for presumed adenocarcinoma
quiz.explain: The first duty with any subsolid nodule seen once is to establish that it is real and persistent, because a large proportion of subsolid opacities are transient: infection, haemorrhage, focal inflammation and organising pneumonia all look like this and are gone in three months. So a repeat thin-section CT at 3 to 6 months precedes any decision. If it persists with a solid component still under 6 mm, annual CT for five years follows, since a persistent part-solid nodule is often on the adenocarcinoma spectrum but grows slowly and the solid part is the invasive part. PET-CT at a 4 mm solid component is below the useful resolution of the technique and lepidic tumour is poorly avid in any case; percutaneous biopsy of a 4 mm target is unreliable; and resecting before persistence is established treats a proportion of patients for pneumonia they have already recovered from.

quiz.prompt: A persistent 12 mm pure ground-glass nodule is referred with a request for PET-CT to confirm that it is benign. The nodule shows no FDG uptake above background lung. How should that result be used?
choices: It does not lower the risk from this appearance
It confirms the nodule is benign, so discharge
It shows the nodule is inflammatory, repeat in 3 months
It means the nodule should be resected without delay
quiz.answer: It does not lower the risk from this appearance
quiz.explain: FDG uptake tracks glucose metabolism and, in practice, viable cell density. A persistent pure ground-glass nodule is characteristically atypical adenomatous hyperplasia, adenocarcinoma in situ or minimally invasive adenocarcinoma, all of which grow along intact alveolar walls with very little cellular bulk, so a negative scan is expected whether the lesion is benign or malignant, and it carries almost no information. Acting on it ends a surveillance programme that the guidance asks to run to five years, and the thing being watched for over those years is the appearance or growth of a solid component. PET-CT earns its place with solid nodules above roughly 8 mm, and even there it has the mirror-image problem of false positives from granulomatous and other inflammatory disease. Small size and low cell density are its two blind spots, and this nodule has both.

quiz.prompt: A CT report flags a new 5 mm nodule. On review it is a smooth, homogeneous, lentiform solid nodule in the right lower zone, in contact with the oblique fissure with its long axis lying along the fissure, and it has a thin linear tail running to the pleura. It was present at the same size on a scan four years earlier. What follow-up is needed?
choices: No follow-up: this is a lymph node
A CT at 12 months for stability
A CT at 3 months, then 12 months
PET-CT to characterise it further
quiz.answer: No follow-up: this is a lymph node
quiz.explain: A typical perifissural nodule is an intrapulmonary lymph node: solid, smooth, homogeneous, oval or triangular, in contact with or within a few millimetres of a fissure or the pleura, usually below the level of the carina, and often with a septal tail running to the pleural surface. In screening cohorts these have proved essentially never to be malignant, and the guidance exempts them from follow-up on morphology alone. Four years of stability settles the matter independently, since two years of unchanged size is the conventional evidence of benignity for a solid nodule. That convention is worth keeping separate in your mind from subsolid disease, where it does not hold: adenocarcinoma in situ can sit unchanged for years, so two years of stability in a ground-glass nodule proves nothing.

quiz.prompt: A 9 mm solid nodule found incidentally contains a focus measuring -70 HU on a region of interest placed on a thin section, together with a coarse central clump of calcification. What follows?
choices: Fat and calcium here indicate a hamartoma
The low attenuation indicates a cavity
This appearance requires PET-CT staging
This warrants CT again in 3 to 6 months
quiz.answer: Fat and calcium here indicate a hamartoma
quiz.explain: Macroscopic fat inside a pulmonary nodule, conventionally in the region of -40 to -120 HU, is close to diagnostic of a hamartoma, and with coarse popcorn-like calcification the diagnosis is secure and the nodule needs no follow-up at all. The rare exceptions worth knowing are lipoid pneumonia and fat-containing metastases from liposarcoma or renal cell carcinoma, which do not resemble this. Two cautions govern the measurement. It must be made on thin sections, because partial volume averaging with adjacent air can fabricate a fat-like value in a small nodule. And the calcification pattern must be one of the benign ones, which are central, laminated, diffusely solid and popcorn: eccentric or stippled calcium does not exclude malignancy, since a carcinoma can engulf a pre-existing granuloma. Recognising the nodule that needs nothing is as much a part of the algorithm as recognising the one that needs everything.

quiz.prompt: A 31-year-old two years after renal transplantation, on tacrolimus and mycophenolate, has three new solid nodules of 4 to 5 mm on a CT performed for fever. A trainee proposes an optional CT at 12 months, quoting the Fleischner recommendations. What is wrong with that?
choices: The guideline excludes patients like this one
The nodules are multiple, so the interval halves
The nodules are too small to be measured reliably
The patient's age puts her in the low-risk column
quiz.answer: The guideline excludes patients like this one
quiz.explain: The 2017 recommendations apply to incidental nodules in immunocompetent patients aged 35 and over who have no known primary malignancy, and they explicitly do not apply within a lung cancer screening programme, where a structured reporting system takes over. This patient fails on two counts, and each on its own would be enough. Immunosuppressed, new nodules with fever are an infection question until proved otherwise, and invasive fungal disease, nocardia, mycobacteria and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder are answered in days by a repeat scan, bronchoscopy or empirical treatment, not in a year. Under 35, the prior probability of lung cancer is low and the accumulated radiation of surveillance is comparatively costly, so benign and infective causes are managed clinically. Knowing when an algorithm does not apply is the part of it that most often gets skipped.

quiz.prompt: A part-solid nodule under annual surveillance measures 15 mm overall on this year's scan and on last year's, but its solid component has gone from 4 mm to 9 mm over those 12 months. The patient has no new symptoms. What should happen?
choices: Refer for PET-CT, biopsy or resection
Continue annual CT to complete five years
Repeat CT at 3 months to confirm growth
Treat for infection and rescan in 6 weeks
quiz.answer: Refer for PET-CT, biopsy or resection
quiz.explain: In a part-solid nodule the solid component is the invasive component, and it drives both the risk and, if this becomes a cancer diagnosis, the T category. A growing solid component, or one reaching 8 mm, takes the nodule out of surveillance and into PET-CT, sampling or resection. The trap the case is built around is that the overall diameter never changed: had only the total size been recorded, the nodule would have been called stable and left for another year, which is why the solid component is measured separately on every study, on the same thin-section lung-window images. Waiting a further three months to confirm growth repeats a measurement already made over a whole year and delays treatment of a lesion that has declared itself. At 9 mm the solid component is also large enough for PET-CT to be informative, which it was not when the component was 4 mm.

quiz.prompt: On a 1 mm axial section an incidental solid nodule measures 7.0 mm along its long axis and 3.8 mm along the perpendicular short axis on the same image. Applying the Fleischner measurement convention, what size in millimetres is recorded for this nodule? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The convention is the average of the long-axis and short-axis diameters obtained on the same image, rounded to the nearest whole millimetre, measured on thin sections in a lung window. Here 7.0 and 3.8 average to 5.4, which is recorded as 5 mm, and that places an elongated nodule whose longest measurement is 7 mm below the 6 mm threshold, so a low-risk patient needs no routine follow-up. Reporting the long axis alone would have committed the same patient to a year of surveillance for the same lesion. The convention exists because it is reproducible rather than because it is the truth about the object: a nodule is not a sphere, and averaging two orthogonal diameters is simply a rule two readers can both follow. Semi-automated volumetry is more reproducible again, and the guidance gives the equivalents, roughly 100 cubic millimetres at 6 mm and 250 at 8 mm, for departments that measure volume instead.

quiz.prompt: A solid nodule has a mean diameter of 6.0 mm. Treating it as a sphere, what mean diameter in millimetres corresponds to exactly one doubling of its volume? Give it to one decimal place. Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Volume scales with the cube of diameter, so a doubling needs a diameter multiplied by the cube root of two, that is 1.26: 6.0 becomes 7.56, or 7.6 mm to one decimal place. The lesson is in how small that step is. A whole doubling of tumour volume shows up as 1.6 mm on a ruler, which is inside the interobserver variability of manual measurement of a small nodule, so a solid nodule can double without any reader being able to prove it, and two readers can disagree about growth that never happened. That is the argument for volumetry, which measures the quantity that is actually doubling, and for long enough intervals that real growth outruns the noise. Volume doubling times of roughly 100 to 400 days characterise most solid lung cancers; much faster than that suggests infection or inflammation, and much slower suggests a benign lesion or an indolent subsolid tumour, whose doubling times commonly run to several years.

quiz.prompt: A solitary pure ground-glass nodule of 9 mm is still present and unchanged on the confirmatory CT performed at 9 months. Counting from the first scan, for how many years in total does the 2017 Fleischner guidance recommend that surveillance continue? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: A solitary ground-glass nodule of 6 mm or more gets a CT at 6 to 12 months to confirm that it persists, then CT every two years out to five years in total. Persistence has ruled out infection and haemorrhage; it has emphatically not ruled out tumour, because the lesions that produce a persistent ground-glass nodule grow so slowly that the two-year stability rule used for solid nodules carries no weight here. Five years is not a claim that risk falls to zero afterwards, but a judgement about the yield of continued scanning against its radiation and cost. What the surveillance is watching for is a change in character rather than a change in size: the appearance of a solid component, or the growth of one, is the event that signals invasion and moves the patient from watching to treatment.

quiz.prompt: The 2017 revision moved the threshold below which no routine follow-up is advised from 4 mm up to 6 mm. Justify that change, and say what it implies for a 5 mm solid nodule in a heavy smoker.
quiz.answer: The evidence, largely from screening cohorts, is that a solid nodule under 6 mm carries a risk of malignancy below about one per cent even in high-risk people, and that a year of CT surveillance changes very little for such a nodule, because growth of that magnitude sits inside the measurement noise and because a cancer that small is usually still curable when it later declares itself. Set against that near-zero yield are real costs: the radiation of repeated scans, the financial cost, the anxiety of being under surveillance, and the cascade of further imaging and procedures that follows a followed nodule. Raising the threshold therefore removes surveillance from a very large number of people with little loss of cancer detection. For a 5 mm nodule in a heavy smoker the guidance offers an optional CT at 12 months rather than requiring one: the judgement is handed to the clinician and the patient, and an upper lobe location, spiculation, emphysema or fibrosis, or a family history are legitimate reasons for an individual to take it.
quiz.explain: A threshold in a guideline is a statement about the balance of harms rather than a claim about biology, and reading it that way explains both the change and the hedging around it. Below 6 mm the yield of surveillance is so low that the harms of scanning dominate, so the recommendation is withdrawn; the nodules did not become safer in 2017. It also explains why the high-risk column says optional rather than recommended: at that risk level the decision is genuinely close, and the guideline declines to make it for the patient. The corollary for reporting is to give the referrer what the decision needs, which is the mean diameter measured by the convention, the solid or subsolid character, the location, the margin, and an explicit statement of which follow-up row the nodule falls in, rather than a bare description of a nodule.

quiz.prompt: A nodule reported as 7 mm last year is reported as 9 mm today, and the patient is referred as growing. Before accepting growth, list the conditions that must match between the two measurements, and say which single technique removes most of the remaining disagreement.
quiz.answer: Both measurements should come from thin sections, ideally 1 mm and at most about 1.5 mm, displayed in a lung window with comparable settings, made by the same convention, which is the average of long and short axis on the same image, and read in the same plane; a nodule measured on a 5 mm series last year against a 1 mm series today will appear to change for purely technical reasons, and partial volume averaging in the thicker series usually understates it. Respiratory phase and patient positioning should be comparable, since a nodule in dependent lung can be measured differently in atelectatic surroundings. Above all, the prior images should be re-measured personally rather than the previous report's number being taken on trust, since the two numbers being compared were produced by different readers. Manual diameter carries an interobserver variability of a millimetre or two, which is the same size as the change being argued about, and semi-automated volumetry is substantially more reproducible: it measures the quantity that actually doubles, and expresses change as a volume doubling time.
quiz.explain: Most reported growth in small nodules is measurement, not biology, and the discipline that prevents the error is comparing like with like and doing the comparison yourself. Two habits carry most of the benefit. First, always open the prior study rather than reading its report, because the number in a report is a different reader's judgement on possibly different data. Second, state the technique the measurement came from in your own report, so that whoever compares next year knows what to match. The deeper point is about what growth means once established: a change in diameter is hard to interpret, whereas a volume doubling time places the lesion on a scale where roughly 100 to 400 days is typical of solid malignancy, faster suggests inflammation, and much slower suggests something indolent or benign.

quiz.prompt: An incidental solid nodule is found on a CT performed for another reason. Put these five decisions in the order that gets the follow-up right, beginning with the one that can stop the algorithm before any measurement is made.
quiz.explain: First, whether the guidance applies to this patient at all: under 35, immunosuppressed, a known primary malignancy, or a nodule found within a screening programme, and it does not, so any table you consult afterwards gives the wrong answer confidently. Second, whether the nodule is already diagnosed by its morphology, since fat with popcorn calcification makes a hamartoma, a benign calcification pattern makes a granuloma, and a typical perifissural nodule makes an intrapulmonary lymph node, and each of these ends the matter with no follow-up at all. Third, solid or subsolid, because the two run on different tables and different timescales. Fourth, the mean diameter by the averaging convention, which selects the row. And last, the patient's risk category, which chooses between columns and, in the smallest band, between an optional scan and none. Risk comes last because it modifies a recommendation rather than generating one, and applying it first is how a heavy smoker with an obvious hamartoma ends up in five years of surveillance.

approach.step: Confirm it is a true nodule, not a perifissural lymph node
approach.detail: A typical perifissural nodule is attached to a fissure, homogeneous, solid, smooth-margined — it needs no follow-up at all.

approach.step: Measure by convention — and keep to one pathway
approach.detail: This block is the BTS pathway: size by volumetry where your PACS supports it, otherwise maximum diameter. Fleischner 2017 instead averages the long and short axis. Do not mix them — averaging against BTS thresholds systematically undersizes the nodule.
Subsolid nodules (pure ground-glass or part-solid) are staged and followed differently from solid nodules, and behave more indolently.
Nodules under the guideline's minimum size need no follow-up; above it, follow-up or risk modelling applies.

approach.step: Run the Brock model where the nodule warrants it
approach.detail: Age, smoking status, nodule size, location, spiculation, family history and emphysema feed a malignancy probability for solid nodules over the threshold, and for subsolid nodules once they have proven stable at 3 months.

approach.step: Add PET-CT and the Herder model selectively
approach.detail: When the Brock score reaches the intermediate range, FDG-avidity on PET-CT refines the probability further (Herder model).

approach.step: Judge growth on volume, not diameter, where volumetry is available
approach.detail: Volume change is a more sensitive growth signal than a change in linear diameter, and shortens the necessary follow-up duration.

measure.how: Percentage change in volume between two scans on the same technique.
Calculated from two volumetric measurements a known interval apart.
measure.cutoff: > 600 days — consider discharge · < 400 days — treat as higher risk of malignancy

measure.how: Total surveillance period depends on the measurement method used.
measure.cutoff: 1 year with volumetry · 2 years with manual 2D measurement

classify.name: BTS pathway for the incidental solid nodule
rows: Discharge. A perifissural nodule > 10 mm or with atypical features warrants consideration of follow-up.
Apply the Brock model for malignancy risk
Repeat CT at 3 months to confirm persistence, then apply the Brock model if it persists

pitfalls: Following a typical perifissural nodule — it is a lymph node, not a nodule to survey, and BTS says so explicitly.
Judging stability by eye on the diameter alone when volumetry is available — a nodule can grow 25% in volume with almost no visible change in diameter.
Running the Brock model on a subsolid nodule before it has proven persistent at 3 months — transient infective or haemorrhagic nodules are excluded first.
Stopping surveillance at 1 year on manual 2D measurements — that duration is only validated for volumetric follow-up; 2D measurement needs the full 2 years.

Reaching for a Lung-RADS category — Lung-RADS is a US lung-cancer-screening scheme, not part of this guideline or the Fleischner 2017 incidental-nodule guideline; do not mix the two frameworks in one report.

radiology_reference.overview: Measure an incidental nodule to the Fleischner convention, judge solid from subsolid, and give the follow-up the guidance recommends or say why it does not apply.
learning_points: Use the recommended plane and a reproducible average diameter.
Solid, part-solid and ground-glass nodules behave differently.
Risk, age and exclusions determine the follow-up pathway.
Review risk context, age and applicable pathway.
Review nodule: lobe, type and mean diameter or volume.
Review solid component of a subsolid nodule.
Review morphology, calcification and perifissural features.
Review growth, comparison interval and follow-up eligibility.
Do not apply an incidental-nodule table to screening, known cancer or immunosuppression without checking its exclusions.

checklist.label: Eligibility
checklist.detail: Check age, immune status, cancer history and screening context.

checklist.label: Nodule type
checklist.detail: Distinguish solid, pure ground glass and part-solid.

checklist.label: Morphology
checklist.detail: Assess margins, fat, calcium, perifissural shape and cystic change.

checklist.label: Measurement
checklist.detail: Document location, mean diameter or consistent volume, and solid component.

checklist.label: Growth
checklist.detail: Use comparable reconstructions and identify the most suspicious lesion in multiple nodules.

measurements.name: Mean diameter
measurements.method: Average long and perpendicular short axes in the plane of greatest dimension; report mm.
measurements.pitfall: Thick sections can create false ground-glass components.

measurements.name: Solid component
measurements.method: Measure separately in a part-solid nodule on a consistent technique.
measurements.pitfall: Whole-nodule stability does not negate growth of the solid component.
